summary: This proposed standard specifies multilateral interconnection at Internet Exchange Points, where three or more BGP speakers exchange routing information through a single intermediary called a route server. The document describes how a route server should behave so participants need fewer individual sessions with one another.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of every neighbor writing to every other neighbor, everyone sends their news to one friendly post office that passes it on to the rest. This explains how that post office should behave.

subtitle: How a route server lets many networks at an exchange point share routes through one BGP broker.

tldr.problem: At a large Internet Exchange Point, setting up a separate BGP session between every pair of participants causes substantial operational scaling problems.
tldr.mechanism: Each participant (a route server client) opens one EBGP session to a route server, which forwards reachability information to the other clients. The route server leaves attributes such as NEXT_HOP and AS_PATH untouched so clients still see the routes as the originators intended.
tldr.outcome: The RFC lists the changes to BGP behavior a route server needs, and describes path hiding, a side effect of per-client policy, with ways to avoid it.

facts.label: Session type
facts.value: EBGP between route server and each client

today: RFC 7947 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its operational companion is RFC 7948.

sections.title: Multilateral Interconnection
sections.content:
Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) give their participants IP interconnection, usually over a shared Layer 2 medium such as Ethernet. The Border Gateway Protocol (RFC 4271) is commonly used to exchange reachability information there. Bilateral EBGP sessions between participants used to be the most common approach, but the overhead of dense interconnection can cause substantial scaling problems at larger IXPs.

Multilateral interconnection uses a third-party broker, the route server, typically run by the IXP operator. Each participant, called a route server client, announces its routes to the route server over EBGP. The route server forwards them to each client according to its configuration. It uses BGP, but it does not forward traffic itself, so it is not a router.

The RFC compares it to a route reflector (RFC 4456) that works over EBGP instead of IBGP. It also warns that the term is used elsewhere for a "route collector" or "route-views server" that gathers feeds for analysis. This document means only the multilateral peering broker. Route server support is not mandatory in BGP implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: If twenty kids all want to swap notes, writing to every other kid is a lot of work. With a route server, everyone gives their notes to one helper, who hands them to the others.

sections.title: How a Route Server Handles Updates
sections.content:
A route server MUST accept all UPDATE messages from each client into its Adj-RIB-In. Policy filters may then keep some of them out of its Loc-RIB or Loc-RIBs. The route server SHOULD run one or more BGP Decision Processes to pick the routes it advertises, and SHOULD forward UPDATE messages from its Loc-RIB or Loc-RIBs to clients as local policy decides.

The server may be configured to give a client several paths for one prefix, or to keep several Loc-RIBs. Both options come back in the path-hiding discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: The post office opens every letter it receives and keeps a copy. Then it decides, using its own rules, which letters to pass along to whom.

sections.title: Attribute Transparency
sections.content:
A route server mostly brokers, so changing attributes could change how clients rank routes and so alter participants' intended policies. Contrary to Section 5 of RFC 4271, route servers SHOULD NOT by default update well-known BGP attributes before passing them on, and SHOULD NOT update optional attributes (transitive or not), unless local IXP operator configuration says so.

  • NEXT_HOP: MUST be passed unmodified, since the route server does not take part in forwarding.
  • AS_PATH: the route server SHOULD NOT prepend its own AS number or modify the path in any way. This is a SHOULD only so legacy clients keep working.
  • MULTI_EXIT_DISC: SHOULD be propagated to other clients, and the route server SHOULD NOT change its value.
  • Communities (Communities and Extended Communities): SHOULD NOT be modified, processed or removed, except as local policy defines. A community meant for the route server itself MAY be modified or removed.
sections.plainLanguage: A good post office delivers letters exactly as written. It does not cross out the return address or add its own name. Only notes addressed to the post office itself get opened and acted on.

sections.title: What Clients Must Accept
sections.content:
Because the route server does not add its AS number, the leftmost AS in the AS_PATH will not equal the route server's AS number. This conflicts with Section 6.3 of RFC 4271, so route server clients need to accept such UPDATE messages.

If a client implements the check, it MUST allow the check to be disabled and SHOULD allow disabling it per peer.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally you expect each letter to name the last person who handled it. Here the post office stays anonymous, so receivers must be told not to worry when its name is missing.

sections.title: Per-Client Policy and Path Hiding
sections.content:
Participants sometimes need to control which other participants receive their routes. With bilateral peering, a network simply skips a session or filters outbound on it. With a route server, only the server can filter in the direction of a client.

Assuming the standard Decision Process, when several clients advertise the same prefix the server picks a single path for all clients. If filtering stops that best path from reaching a particular client, that client gets no path for the prefix, even if another path would have been allowed. This is path hiding.

The RFC's example: a prefix arrives via AS2 and AS4, AS2's route wins, but AS2's policy forbids sending it to AS1. AS1 never receives a path, although a valid one via AS4 was available. This happens because the Decision Process runs only once for all clients. Path hiding occurs only on servers that use per-client policy control.

This part of the RFC (Section 2.3 and its subsections) is informational and not part of the normative specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The post office picks one favorite letter about a topic and sends it to everyone. If a friend is not allowed to get that letter, they get nothing about the topic, even though another letter would have been fine.

sections.title: Ways to Avoid Path Hiding
sections.content:
The RFC describes three approaches.

Multiple RIBs. The most portable method is for the route server to do a best-path calculation per client after that client's policies are applied. This uses per-client Loc-RIBs with filtering between the Adj-RIB-In and each Loc-RIB. Implementations may keep unfiltered paths in a global Loc-RIB and store per-client Loc-RIBs as deltas. It assumes nothing about client capabilities.

Diverse BGP paths (RFC 6774). The server uses a separate BGP session to the client for each path. The number of paths is limited by the number of sessions, so path hiding is not always eliminated, and many extra sessions may hurt server performance.

BGP ADD-PATH (RFC 7911). Several paths for one prefix travel on a single session. Both the server and its clients must support it. If ADD-PATH is negotiated in both directions, a client could send inactive, invalid or suboptimal paths to the server, so servers should use send-only mode, which negotiates receive-only mode from the client.

Operations advice is in a separate document, RFC 7948.
sections.plainLanguage: Fixes: give each friend their own personal pile of letters, send several envelopes at once, or let one envelope hold several letters. Each fix has its own costs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Path hiding can, in some circumstances, be used to proactively block third-party path announcements from other clients, so operators should mitigate it.

The AS_PATH check is normally enabled to catch malformed AS paths and to detect BGP loops. Disabling it risks propagating corrupted UPDATE messages and forming routing loops. Participants SHOULD NOT disable it unless needed to establish sessions with a route server and, if possible, should disable it only for peers that are route servers. Operators should also consider the practices in RFC 7454.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky friend could use the rules to keep other people's news from reaching you. And turning off the check for odd-looking letters means you could pass along broken or looping ones.
